Data-types for spIBDerverse functions

Source: vignettes/data-types.Rmd
data-types.Rmd
library(spIBDerverse)
library(igraph)
#> 
#> Attaching package: 'igraph'
#> The following objects are masked from 'package:stats':
#> 
#>     decompose, spectrum
#> The following object is masked from 'package:base':
#> 
#>     union
library(sf)
#> Linking to GEOS 3.12.1, GDAL 3.8.4, PROJ 9.4.0; sf_use_s2() is TRUE

In the spIBDerverse package, we have two structures that are used by most of the functions, and hence by the spibder_app() which gives the shiny GUI.

The most common object and the primary one for the shiny app is an igraph object. This is the primary data structure used by the igraph object. @lst-igraph loads an example network and shows it structure.

Notice that to ensure that we do not have clashes if a user has already add centrality measures, we often also add them using the function add_centrality_measures() which adds the common centrality measures to the igraph object but with names like .degree, the use of a prefix of . should hopefully stop any clashes.

data(example_network)
example_network
#> IGRAPH 05e5699 UN-- 40 123 -- 
#> + attr: genetic_sex (v/c), site (v/c), name (v/c), .degree (v/n),
#> | .closeness (v/n), .betweenness (v/n), .eigencentrality (v/n),
#> | .louvain (v/c), .louvain_weighted (v/c), .eigen (v/c),
#> | .eigen_weighted (v/c), .label_prop (v/c), .label_prop_weighted (v/c),
#> | lat (v/n), long (v/n), wij (e/n), edge_type (e/c)
#> + edges from 05e5699 (vertex names):
#>  [1] 1--2  1--5  1--6  1--11 1--15 1--26 1--29 1--31 1--39 2--7  2--10 2--11
#> [13] 2--14 2--19 2--26 2--34 2--39 3--5  3--12 3--31 3--33 3--38 4--28 4--34
#> [25] 5--7  5--11 5--14 5--15 5--30 5--34 5--37 5--39 6--14 6--20 6--27 6--31
#> [37] 6--33 7--8  7--11 7--14 7--19 7--20 7--22 7--25 7--29 7--33 7--34 7--36
#> + ... omitted several edges

If you would like to visualise the network on a map, then a node attibute for longitude and latitude is necessary.

For some of the plotting functions for networks on maps, we also use a network sf object. @lst-sf illustrates this object. We see that is is list that contains two objects both of sf types, a node object that contains information about the node positions represented as points, and an edge object that contains the information for the edges represented as linestring objects.

A network sf object can be obtained from an igraph object as illustrated in @lst-create.

example_sf <- convert_sf(
  example_network,
  "lat",
  "long",
  landscape = TRUE
)

The package spIBDerverse has the following example networks built-in:

  • example_network,
  • example_network_2,
  • example_network_3,
  • example_sf, and
  • dist_network.
